papers.title: Towards Invariance to Node Identifiers in Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are known to have limited expressive power, due to their message passing structure. One mechanism for circumventing this limitation is to add unique node identifiers (IDs), which break the symmetries that underlie the expressivity limitation. In this work, we highlight a key limitation of the ID framework, and propose an approach for addressing it. We begin by observing that the final output of the GNN should clearly not depend on the specific IDs used. We then show that in practice the network does in fact depend on the IDs, which is undesirable. Invariance to node IDs may be enforced in several ways, and we discuss their theoretical properties. We then propose a novel regularization method that effectively enforces ID invariance to the network. Extensive evaluations on both real-world and synthetic tasks demonstrate that our approach significantly improves ID invariance and, in turn, often boosts generalization performance.

content.paper_summary: This paper presents a novel method in addressing a critical issue in the expressiveness of GNN (Graph Neural Networks). They introduce the fundamental limits of MPNN (message passing neural networks) in its expressiveness and found out the issue with an existing method in bridging the expressiveness gap (RNI, random node initialization). They then fixed this gap with ICON (ID-Invariance through Contrast), and provided empirical and theoretical analyses on how and why practical models fail to learn invariance with the added expressiveness property and how ICON learns these behaviors.
content.critical_strengths:
1. substantial improvements over the baseline RNI results in many axes
2. good theoretical analyses
3. clean writing
content.critical_weaknesses:
1. mixed improvements compared with baseline GNNs (GraphConv, GIN, GAT, TransformerConv, and GraphGPS without RNI and ICON): I am not observing significant improvements to the baseline methods. The performance of the models in table 2 are mostly just matching regular baseline GNNs without the author's methods, and that actually adding the expressive baseline method (RNI) for becoming more expressive hurts most of the time. This entails a question that, if the expressive baseline is significantly worse than the baseline GNNs and the authors just try to fix the expressive baseline to match the baseline GNNs, what's the right interpretation on the benefits that this paper introduces? Why do we need this method if it is a "fix" to a bug in the expressive baseline? 
2. Convergence and Generalization claims: I am not seeing the matched comparison with baseline GNNs.
content.questions_for_authors:
1. Can you explain why ICON helps very little with downstream graph task performance (compared with GNN baseline)? I am seeing Table 2 showing mixed improvements on various tasks compared with baseline GNN methods(GraphConv, GIN, GAT, TransformerConv, and GraphGPS). It would also be nice if the authors can report the compute and flop required for training the methods so that we can be certain on the validity on the comparison. 
2. Regarding the claim on faster convergence: could you also compare with GNN baseline? 
3. It'd be nice if the authors could justify why it is so critical to be more expressive with a GNN method, when its performance only matches that of the baseline GNN methods. The added benefits are on generalization and convergence speed, but it is not cleanly compared with baseline GNNs.

content.paper_summary: This paper proposes ICON, an ID-invariance regularization method that addresses overfitting and degraded generalization caused by GNNs over-relying on specific random node ID values when enhancing expressive power. Experimental results show that ICON consistently outperforms random node initialization (RNI) across various GNN architectures.
content.critical_strengths:
(1) This paper proposes a simple yet effective method for enhancing GNN expressivity with minimal architectural modifications.
(2) This paper provides theoretical analysis of the relationship between ID invariance and GNN expressivity.
(3) This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through experiments on multiple datasets and GNN architectures.
content.critical_weaknesses:
(1) Although the paper addresses an interesting problem, the proposed method essentially relies on a conventional consistency regularization term to reduce the model's dependence on specific random node ID values, resulting in limited methodological novelty.
(2) While ICON achieves promising improvements over the original random node initialization (RNI) method, comparisons with other node ID-based methods are missing. Moreover, most evaluated GNN architectures are relatively outdated, leaving its effectiveness compared with recent GNN architectures and node ID-based methods unclear.
(3) The paper lacks further ablation studies to evaluate the effects of applying regularization at different layers or multiple layers. Additionally, ICON appears to show limited improvements over the original GNNs on some smaller graphs or datasets, which warrants further investigation.
content.questions_for_authors:
(1) The authors are encouraged to compare ICON with more recent node ID-based methods and GNN architectures to further validate its effectiveness.
(2) Additional ablation studies are recommended to better demonstrate the effectiveness of applying regularization specifically at the final layer.
(3) The authors should provide a more thorough discussion of ICON's performance across different graph and dataset sizes, particularly on small graphs and datasets.

content.paper_summary: While GNNs naturally provide permutation invariance over nodes, the authors aim to enhance their expressive power by introducing node IDs as additional node features. However, random node ID features may break permutation invariance. Therefore, the authors propose introducing regularization terms during training to preserve this invariance while incorporating node ID features.
content.critical_strengths:
The experimental benchmarking includes multiple baselines and provides comprehensive results demonstrating improvements on small-scale datasets.

The overall flow of the paper is natural and easy to follow. The intermediate results effectively motivate the proposed idea and demonstrate the authors' clear reasoning behind its development.
content.critical_weaknesses:
One concern is that, although the proposed regularization term encourages node ID invariance, it is unclear whether the final node features are strictly constrained to guarantee this property. How do the authors ensure that all permutations of node IDs produce the same results? Does the training process consider all possible node ID permutations when computing the regularization term?

Additionally, for more expressive GNN architectures that can distinguish graphs beyond 1-WL, how can the proposed regularization term guarantee node ID invariance on input graphs distinguishable by 3-WL? For example, if you apply this term to GIN, which is proven to have 1-WL test expressiveness, can adding this regularization term distinguish a 3-WL test graph?
content.questions_for_authors:
For Definition 4.1, would the authors mind clarifying the definition of the symbol \(S\)? Does \(S\) represent the set of all graphs? Additionally, for the matrix $\(I \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}\)$, could the authors clarify the definition of \(r\)?

I also have a question regarding the expressive power of the proposed method. With the introduction of the new node features, can the expressive power of GNNs be improved beyond the 1-WL or even 3-WL test? If so, could the authors provide further theoretical justification?

Besides real-world graph datasets, have the authors evaluated the proposed method on synthetic datasets specifically designed for WL tests? Additionally, have the authors compared their method with other GNN architectures whose expressive power has been theoretically established beyond 1-WL and up to 3-WL? What are the advantages and disadvantages of the proposed method compared to these approaches?

papers.title: FoAReD: Foreground-guided Attention Reallocation Decoding for Comprehensive Image Captioning
papers.abstract: Despite their strong image captioning capabilities, VLMs often fail to capture fine-grained details in complex scenes. We find that this issue is associated with insufficient utilization of visual information during autoregressive decoding, where attention is dominated by redundant background and sink tokens. To address this issue, we propose FoAReD, a training-free image captioning framework that enhances visual information utilization through attention contrastive decoding.  Specifically, FoAReD employs foreground-guided attention reallocation to construct a contrastive attention condition.  During autoregressive decoding, the contrastive and original attention conditions are contrasted to enhance the generation preference toward informative visual details. Experiments on CompreCap and CaptionQA across multiple VLMs show that FoAReD consistently improves both caption comprehensiveness and accuracy.

content.paper_summary: This paper incorporates foreground-background discrimination with attention contrastive decoding for image captioning. In particular, it locates sink visual tokens, tokens likely belonging to backgrounds, and attention heads concentrating on foreground with heuristics and prior methods. These identified tokens and attention heads are then used to define the attention maps used for contrastive decoding. Experimental results on several public models show that the proposed method achieves favorable improvements across different settings.
content.critical_strengths:
(1) It is a promising direction to enhance models’ reasoning capabilities by redirecting their attention to pertinent visual information. 

(2) The method shows consistent improvements over three baselines, and appears to generate captions with more details.

(3) The paper proposes extensive ablation study, which facilitates understanding the contribution of individual components.
content.critical_weaknesses:
(1) It is not a new idea to redirect models’ attention. While prior work may not specifically emphasize explicit discrimination between foreground and background, a direct comparison with quantitative evaluation is still important here. For instance, do existing attention reallocation methods fail to differentiate foreground and background? What’s the corresponding classification accuracy? Why is the proposed heuristic-based approach better than prior work?

(2) Related to the previous comment. Looking at Table 1, it appears that the improvement achieved by the proposed method is relatively incremental compared to prior methods. It is therefore unclear how advantageous is the explicit discrimination between foreground and background.

(3) Several key comparisons in the paper are rather incomplete in my opinion. Specifically, Table 2 compares the visual token classifications with the proposed method on different backbones, without involving any prior methods. Similarly, Table 4 focuses on hallucination score but no baseline/prior method is compared. Table 3 compares Qwen3 VL 4B with the proposed method against Qwen3 VL 8B, but fails short of analyzing the scaling capabilities of the method, e.g., what’s the performance of different methods on models with increasing scales? 

(4) Table 8 shows that redirecting attention from sink tokens to visual tokens achieves over 80% of the improvement for the full methods. As discussed in Section 2, there is a body of research on utilizing/alleviating attention sink, and some recent models (e.g., DINOv3) have shown to be less prone to sink tokens. How would the proposed method be helpful for these more recent vision models?

(5) The paper only provides two qualitative examples on how the method helps image captioning. However, neither of the examples directly show how attention reallocation, with a focus on differentiating foreground and background, is involved in the inference process. For example, captions generated by the proposed method seem to contain more details, but without a visualization of the corresponding attention, it is uncertain where these additional details are attributed to and whether it is genuinely about background removal. I would also expect some quantitative scores here about how the method shifts attention from background to foreground, and how the foreground attention is linked to the generated captions.
content.questions_for_authors:
(1) Please justify the key advantages of the proposed method over related work on attention reallocation, and directly compare them with attention distribution.

(2) How does the proposed method improve over previous ones in terms of addressing incorrect attention allocation, hallucination, and scaling? Please refer to my comments on the weaknesses.

(3) How does the method work with vision models with fewer or no sink tokens?

(4) Please consider incorporating additional qualitative analysis and quantitative analysis on the relationship between shift in attention distribution and its impacts on generated captions.

content.paper_summary: The authors argue that VLMs fails to capture fine grained details in complex scenes because VLMs insufficiently utilize visual information. The authors attribute this to attention being concentrated on background or sink tokens in later layer. To address this, the authors propose FoAReD, a contrastive decoding method that uses logits generated from attention re-allocation toward foreground tokens.
content.critical_strengths: None
content.critical_weaknesses:
**Comparison with directly related prior works on attention steering/re-allocation is insufficient, and the findings claimed as contributions are already known.**

The authors suggest that existing methods improve captioning by introducing external supervision or guidance. However, many works already utilize internal visual representations such as attention for better utilization of  visual information. 

PAI [1] also steers the attention to image tokens during decoding and combines it with contrastive decoding, which is close to the attention contrastive decoding proposed in this paper. 

SPARC [2] demonstrates that VLMs’ attention to key visual tokens weakens and attention shows a noisy pattern (concentrating on irrelevant(background) or sink tokens) especially during long context text generation in detailed image captioning tasks, and it selectively amplifies the attention to key visual tokens.

ASCD [3] addresses weak visual dependency by identifying key heads based on the text-to-image attention ratio and reallocating attention to strengthen these heads. It then performs contrastive decoding between the resulting logits and the logits obtained from decoding with weakened visual dependency. 

Therefore, FoAReD’s components, foreground-guided attention reallocation(FAR), visual token classification(VTC), and attention contrastive decoding(ACD) have all been proposed in prior works in a broad sense, so the novelty is limited. Morerover, none of these methods are compared in the experiments. 

Also, it is already known that attention to the relevant visual tokens in VLMs is high in the mid layers and low in the later layers. Furthermore, the later layers are considered to be the textual decoding stage, so the low visual attention in these later layers is not necessarily a problem [4,5].

[1] Liu et al. Paying More Attention to Images: A Training-Free Method for Alleviating Hallucination in LVLMs. ECCV2024

[2] Jung et al. Visual Attention Never Fades: Selective Progressive Attention ReCalibration for Detailed Image Captioning in Multimodal Large Language Models. ICML 2025

[3] Wang et al. ASCD: Attention-Steerable Contrastive Decoding for Reducing Hallucination in MLLM. AAAI 2026

[4] Jiang et al. Devils in Middle Layers of Large Vision-Language Models: Interpreting, Detecting and Mitigating Object Hallucinations via Attention Lens. CVPR 2025

[5] Zhang et al. MLLMs Know Where to Look: Training-free Perception of Small Visual Details with Multimodal LLMs. ICLR 2025
content.questions_for_authors:
1. There are too many hyperparameters, which is concern. Currently, ablations are provided only for some of the parameters on Qwen3-VL-4B and CompreCap. Could the authors provide ablations for all parameters, and on other models and benchmarks?

2. The choice of layers for attention reallocation seems to be the most important, however there is no description of it. Could the authors describe the used layer and add an ablation on the layer?

3. The authors suggest that the background tokens have small L2 norms of visual token features. This contradicts prior work [6], which shows that tokens whose ViT feature norm is high often contain globally redundant visual information (background). Could the authors provide further explanation related with this?

4. Pruning on the background tokens seems to be orthogonal to the baselines in the main experiments. Therefore, applying the token pruning method only to FoAReD seems unfair. Also, since latency is strongly affected by response length, could the authors measure latency in s/token?

[6] Gong et al. DAMRO: Dive into the Attention Mechanism of LVLM to Reduce Object Hallucination. EMNLP 2024

content.paper_summary: FoAReD is a training-free framework for comprehensive image captioning. It uses feature norms to identify background candidates, prunes redundant tokens, and selectively reallocates attention from background and sink tokens to foreground tokens, favoring less-attended ones. Logit-level contrastive decoding amplifies the resulting prediction changes. Experiments across three VLM backbones report improved CompreCap and CaptionQA performance and reduced AMBER hallucination scores, supported by token-classification evaluation, ablations, and a length-controlled comparison. The method requires internal attention access and additional inference computation.
content.critical_strengths:
1. Cross-model gains with supporting controls. CompreCap Unified improves by 2.00, 1.91, and 5.30 points on Qwen3-VL-4B, LLaVA-v1.6-7B, and InternVL3-2B, respectively, alongside lower AMBER hallucination scores. The Qwen3-VL length-controlled comparison suggests that longer captions alone do not explain the improvement. Together, these results support broader caption coverage without worse performance on the reported hallucination benchmark.

2. A useful training-free approach with competitive reported latency. Selective foreground reallocation and contrastive decoding require neither parameter updates nor external visual experts. FoAReD outperforms VCD in Unified score with slightly lower reported latency on all three backbones, supporting its practical value beyond simply adding computation to the base model.
content.critical_weaknesses:
1. The core intervention is not fully specified. Sections 3.2.2 – 3.2.3 provide head-classification statistics and recipient-side attention increments, but do not explicitly specify the classification thresholds and complete decision rules, source-side deductions, or handling of foreground/sink overlap. Although renormalization is stated, the complete source-to-recipient update is not spelled out. These details affect reproducibility and verification of the proposed mechanism. This is a specification concern, not evidence of an implementation error.

2. Ablation interpretation and evaluation protocols remain unclear. Table 6 does not fully define how FAR and ACD are disabled. If “ACD disabled” corresponds to α = 0 in Equation (3) under otherwise identical settings, its score of 65.70 appears inconsistent with the approximately 65.3 read from Figure 7e. Different configurations could explain this, but the relationship is not clarified. Actual evaluation sample sizes, decoding/scoring configurations, and hyperparameter selection and transfer procedures are also insufficiently specified. These gaps limit attribution of component gains and assessment of robustness despite the positive overall results.
content.questions_for_authors:
1. Intervention specification: Please provide the complete rules underlying Weakness 1, distinguishing inherited settings from modifications and specifying the renormalization scope. Does background detection use vision-encoder or post-projector features?

2. Ablation correspondence: What is retained or replaced when FAR and ACD are disabled, and do both branches share the same pruned tokens? How does α = 0 relate to “ACD disabled,” and what configuration differences, if any, explain the corresponding results in Table 6 and Figure 7e?

3. Evaluation and cost protocols: Please specify the evaluation and tuning settings underlying Weakness 2 and any generation/scoring randomness. Paired uncertainty estimates, if available, would help assess robustness. For latency, please report hardware, batch size, output lengths, and timing scope, and reconcile the “no additional computational costs” claim with the acknowledged overhead.

papers.title: Zero-Sum Bias Corrections for Confounding by Indication in Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Although offline reinforcement learning promises more personalized treatment regimes in clinical care, challenges remain when action- and outcome-relevant information goes unrecorded in the data used to train policies. Standard value-based offline reinforcement learning methods converge to the observational value of actions and conflate the reason the action was chosen with its effect. Clinical data commonly suffers from confounding by indication, where patients with unrecorded indicators of disease severity both receive more aggressive treatment and experience worse outcomes. This biases naive learners, undervaluing life-saving treatments while overvaluing inaction. Many confounding-robust offline reinforcement learning methods impose bounds that further penalize treatment, while others require strict identification conditions that may be false in practice. In both cases, the learned policy can collapse and fail to provide any patient-specific targeting at all. We introduce an offline reinforcement learning algorithm to correct the training targets under static confounders. Our correction is derived from an omitted-variable-bias factorization and approximates the bias by the product of two components estimated from the full trajectory history, with the direction of the correction given by the data as the sign of a within-trajectory covariance. As per-action biases at a state provably cancel, we constrain our correction to be zero-sum across actions so that value is redistributed rather than uniformly suppressed. Across three synthetic medical environments, one fit to real clinical dynamics, our method produces higher-value policies than competing deconfounding and offline reinforcement learning approaches. Where conservative baselines collapse, our method continues to differentiate between patients.

papers.title: Persistent4D: A Training-Free Streaming World Model with persistent 4D memory
papers.abstract: A visual world model must let an agent apply an action and predict spatio-temporally consistent future observations, which requires both precise camera-controllable generation and a spatial memory that persists across steps. Existing approaches each solve only half of the problem. Controllable-video and interactive world models typically take a strongly pre-trained video generator and further train or fine-tune an action-/camera-control signal on top of it, which demands substantial compute and large paired video–action datasets, and still lacks a persistent geometric memory—so long rollouts drift and revisited viewpoints are not reproduced. Feed-forward 4D reconstruction, in contrast, is training-free but can only re-project already-observed content and cannot hallucinate the disocclusions exposed by a new viewpoint. We present Persistent 4D Memory, a fully training-free streaming world model—we train, fine-tune, and distill nothing, not even a camera-control adapter—that couples an off-the-shelf feed-forward reconstructor with an off-the-shelf video-diffusion inpainter through a cross-round, per-frame 4D point-cloud memory. Each round renders the memory from the target camera (camera control by construction), lets the off-the-shelf generator fill the shrinking disocclusion holes, then re-reconstructs the completed clip under the known camera and fuses the newly revealed content back into memory. This yields three properties: (i) near-zero camera-following error without any camera-conditioning training; (ii) cross-round fusion makes the rollout cycle-consistent—turning away and back reproduces the original view, with hole area dropping from about 58% for a memory-less baseline to under 12%; and (iii) because geometry offloads the vast majority of content and the generator fills only small holes, a single off-the-shelf (community-accelerated) generator suffices for real time—up to ∼20 FPS with a causal streaming back-end—while we train nothing ourselves. We further propose cycle-consistency as an evaluation protocol for world models.

papers.title: Simple Agentic Memory for Generalist Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Visual-memory systems commonly retain or compress past observations. Robot control additionally requires interaction-derived state that no individual frame may explicitly represent, such as persistent identity relations, accumulated progress, or ordered procedures. We introduce Simple Agentic Robot Memory (SimpleARM), a training-free memory layer for frozen generalist robot policies. From the task instruction, SimpleARM specifies what to monitor; frozen perceptual tools maintain compact typed state online; structured access retrieves that state only when a proposed subgoal depends on history; and current-view grounding resolves recalled entities before execution. We evaluate SimpleARM on RoboMME, a benchmark of memory-dependent robot manipulation tasks that require history information no longer available in the current observation. Across all 16 tasks and three policy seeds, SimpleARM achieves 67.17% mean success, compared with 44.51% for the strongest non-oracle baseline. Matched ablations show mechanism specificity: removing relation, reference, progress, or route state produces large losses where the affected state is retrieved for control, while largely sparing other tasks. These results support a state-based view of robot memory: effective memory for control is not simply retained visual history, but compact task-relevant state derived from the interaction history.

content.paper_summary: SimpleARM adds memory for the current episode to a frozen grounded-subgoal predictor and GroundSG VLA. Before execution, an instruction-only VLM specifies candidate entities, progress variables and readers. Perception tools maintain verified identity/container relations and event counts, as well as demonstrated routes. The structural gate allows a read only for compatible subgoal fields; a remembered entity is grounded in the current view when it needs a coordinate. Across all 16 RoboMME tasks and three policy seeds, success is 67.17%, compared with 44.51% for FrameSamp. Matched component removals and failure analyses examine which states matter, and when the policy actually accesses them.
content.critical_strengths:
I found the distinction between maintaining state and using it for control useful. In Figure 3 and Tables 8 to 11, removing route state costs 68 points on average across the two route tasks. Elsewhere, the system can maintain the same state with little effect from its removal because it is never retrieved. The identity-tool experiment makes a similar comparison between retrieved bindings and active but unused ones. The tools and state types are familiar, but these experiments say something concrete about how to connect memory to a robot policy.

The episode-matched FrameSamp comparison is also fairly convincing: 254 episodes succeed only with SimpleARM, against 81 that succeed only with FrameSamp. I appreciate the discussion of accepted but incorrect bindings, including the distinction between internal verification and ground truth, and that StopCube's 0% result remains in the evaluation. I lean weak accept for the system and mechanism analysis, though I would narrow the claim about generality.
content.critical_weaknesses:
The dependence on RoboMME's interface still bothers me. Appendix A.1 describes lexical tests on the subgoal text, and A.3 uses calibrated colour predicates and event parsers. In Figure 12, the parser reads pure-red demonstration cues and maps directions through a fixed camera convention. Instruction rewording costs 17.8 points in Table 12. This is a separate configuration, so it needs some caution, but the size of the loss is concerning. The evidence is stronger for this particular RoboMME implementation than for carrying the instruction-conditioned memory layer to a new task family. I would find a small held-out test with unchanged parsers more useful here than simply another large benchmark.

It is also difficult to assign the full 22.66-point gain to memory, since the system adds perception and subgoal correction. As the authors note, VideoUnmask and BinFill are not very sensitive to the tested removals. Neither the PickHighlight mark reader nor current-view grounding has a separate ablation. The matched removals support several specific mechanisms, but leave part of the system-level gain unexplained. The final component removals use only policy seed 11; the separate identity-tool and no-flow comparisons omit SAM, and the matched FrameSamp runs use different hosts. The paper is careful to document these distinctions. They make me put much more weight on the large effects localized to the relevant tasks than on the small differences.
content.questions_for_authors:
1. Can you separate failures in planner output from failures in the structural reader under instruction rewording? I would like to see a matched test with the final configuration fixed.

2. How much improvement remains with the same perception and grounding tools but persistent memory disabled? A separate mark-reader removal would also help identify which gains come from history.

3. For a held-out task using the same objects in a new combination of historical relations, what would need to change in the schema, event predicates or access rules?

content.paper_summary: The paper argues that robot memory should not be framed as selecting or compressing past observations, but as maintaining policy-sufficient state induced by an action–observation history: persistent identity relations, accumulated progress, and ordered procedures. On this view, the relevant information often lives in no single frame, so memory budget is not the binding constraint. From this framing the authors build SimpleARM, a training-free memory layer wrapped around a frozen hierarchical robot stack.
content.critical_strengths:
1."Robot memory is a problem of maintaining the task-relevant state induced by an action–observation history" is a clear, defensible position, and prior RoboMME evidence makes the motivation concrete rather than rhetorical. The paper is arguing against a real, currently dominant default.
2.Exactly ten LM calls per episode, all before the first action, plus 2.02 s/episode of perception tools, itemised by component. Nonparametric, episode-scoped memory with M0 reset. There is a real path to deployment here.
3.16 tasks, 3 seeds, 50 episodes per task per seed are sufficient. And, the authors retraining and evaluating their own RecentN+ModuL recent-frame baselines at matched protocol Reporting both aggregate and paired-episode views is good practice.
content.critical_weaknesses:
1.The headline comparison is not memory-vs-no-memory within one system. SimpleARM does not merely add a memory layer: it adds an entire frozen perception stack and control interface that the comparison baselines do not possess.
2.RecentN+ModuL variants are each trained once and evaluated at three policy seeds, so the three rounds are not independent training runs and cannot estimate training variance.
3.There is no code/model/prompt availability statement anywhere I could find. 
4.Table 1's "required state" labels are explicitly not mutually exclusive and are derived from task semantics; several of the largest wins (VideoUnmask 96.0 vs 32.7) have no corresponding ablation, so the biggest contributors to the headline are the least attributed.
content.questions_for_authors:
1. Please re-run no route state and agent-decided access at 2–3 policy seeds, so the central specificity claim does not rest on a single seed.
2.How much of the Permanence gain depends on colour-based identity? A short probe with colour-neutral or colour-relabelled objects would tell the reader whether the maintained "identity" is semantic or chromatic.

content.paper_summary: The paper introduces SimpleARM, a training-free memory layer around a frozen grounded-subgoal predictor and VLA policy. An instruction-only stage proposes what to monitor; perception tools and event predicates maintain entity/relation, progress, and ordered-route state; structural access supplies compatible historical information to a proposed subgoal, with current-view grounding when needed. On all 16 RoboMME tasks over three policy seeds, the system obtains 67.17% success versus 44.51% for the strongest reported non-oracle baseline. Matched component removals identify large, task-specific contributions from several maintained variables and from constrained access. The contribution is an effective robot-memory system and its empirical analysis; the approximate policy-sufficiency equation is a design objective rather than a demonstrated general sufficiency result.
content.critical_strengths:
1. Substantial gains across the full benchmark. Evaluation covers all 16 tasks over three seeds, with 542/800 versus 369/800 successes in matched testing. Gains are strongest on Permanence and Reference, while Counting weaknesses are also reported.
2. Informative matched ablations. Component removals cause large, task-specific losses. Replacing structural access with VLM-based decisions reduces overall success by 11.88 points, supporting the value of both maintained states and constrained access.
3. Transparent empirical analysis. The paper distinguishes internal verification from correctness, diagnostic associations from causal evidence, and supplementary controls from final-method ablations. Visual traces clarify how memory affects actions.
content.critical_weaknesses:
Limited evidence of generality. The implementation relies on RoboMME-specific phrase tests, parsing rules, and appearance vocabulary. Instruction rewording substantially reduces performance in a different configuration; a final-configuration paraphrase test is needed to assess robustness.

Incomplete attribution of gains. The ablations establish component usefulness but do not isolate instruction-driven planning from fixed monitoring with the same tools. A matched control disabling all historical state is also missing, so the full 22.66-point gain cannot be attributed to the memory abstraction alone.

Missing implementation details. This paper lacks complete prompts, reader schemas, access tests, and event/demo parsing rules. The configuration differences behind Table 12 also need clarification to support reproduction.
content.questions_for_authors:
1. With the final tool and access stack held fixed, what is the gain from instruction-conditioned monitoring over a fixed or keyword-based monitoring policy? Please clarify how the Table 12 control differs from the final system; a targeted matched comparison would be particularly informative.
2. Does the final system retain its gains under semantics-preserving instruction rewording? Can you separate sensitivity in the instruction-only memory planner from sensitivity in the frozen composer and structural phrase matching?
3. Can you provide the complete prompts, line widths, schemas, access predicates, and demonstration/event parser specifications, together with the development data or procedure used to set these rules and thresholds?
4. Is there a matched control that disables all cross-time state while retaining the same frozen composer/VLA and current-view tools? If unavailable, how should the gains on VideoUnmask and BinFill, which are relatively insensitive to the tested removals, be interpreted?

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the strengths of our work. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestions and address the remaining concerns and questions below. We have completed additional matched controls and clarified the scope of the formulation and its RoboMME instantiation. We look forward to further discussion.

## W1 / Q2: Generality and instruction rewording

> **W1:** The implementation relies on RoboMME-specific phrase tests, parsing rules, and appearance vocabulary. Instruction rewording substantially reduces performance in a different configuration; a final-configuration paraphrase test is needed to assess robustness.
> **Q2:** Does the final system retain its gains under semantics-preserving instruction rewording? Can you separate sensitivity in the instruction-only memory planner from sensitivity in the frozen composer and structural phrase matching?

**Memory-side paraphrase test.** Across 800 matched episodes, success drops from **523/800 (65.38%)** with canonical instructions to **488/800 (61.00%)** with rewording (−4.38 points, 92 canonical-only and 57 rewrite-only successes, exact McNemar $p=0.0052$).

Each of 16 tasks uses two rewrite templates (25 episodes each). We checked the manifest for preserved objects, counts, order and event references. Runtime assertions check canonical environment and composer inputs. Only specification and repetition queries receive the rewrite. Demonstration parsers retain canonical text. The retrieval compiler votes over responses to three line wrappings of one prompt.

**Structural access diagnostic.** We selected ten logged coordinate subgoals spanning seven historical references and three current-view actions. With coordinates and memory held fixed, canonical and syntax-compatible wording match **10/10** intended decisions. Reordered wording misses all seven historical references and correctly skips retrieval in the three current-view cases (**3/10**).

**Relation to Table 12.** The earlier pre-unified system pooled **416 matched pairs** from four handwritten templates per episode on **8 tasks × 13 episodes** at seed 7. Its runtime substitution rebound colours and recognised counts and could fall back to canonical text. The current test passes literal, episode-specific rewrites to the final unified system over all 16 tasks. The two effects (**−17.8** and **−4.38 points**) come from different implementations, rewrites and episode sets.


## W2 / Q4: Attribution to historical state
> **W2:** The ablations establish component usefulness but do not isolate instruction-driven planning from fixed monitoring with the same tools. A matched control disabling all historical state is also missing, so the full 22.66-point gain cannot be attributed to the memory abstraction alone.
> **Q4:** Is there a matched control that disables all cross-time state while retaining the same frozen composer/VLA and current-view tools? If unavailable, how should the gains on VideoUnmask and BinFill, which are relatively insensitive to the tested removals, be interpreted?

We added the corresponding control over 800 matched episodes, bypassing SimpleARM's entity, reference, mark, progress and route stores and their subgoal corrections, including historical phase corrections. It retains the frozen composer and VLA, native demonstration and subgoal context, grasp-gated detector refinement and the segment coordinate cache. Success falls from **523/800 to 276/800 (−30.88 points)**, with **282 full-only and 35 removal-only successes** (exact McNemar $p=4.1\times10^{-49}$).


## W3 / Q3: Reproducibility and development procedure
> **W3:** This paper lacks complete prompts, reader schemas, access tests, and event/demo parsing rules. The configuration differences behind Table 12 also need clarification to support reproduction.
> **Q3:** Can you provide the complete prompts, line widths, schemas, access predicates, and demonstration/event parser specifications, together with the development data or procedure used to set these rules and thresholds?

We developed the access rules from RoboMME subgoal syntax and the event parsers from task-specific visual cues in saved rollouts. The colour verifier uses RGB references calibrated offline from oracle-labelled image patches. The retained records do not identify the calibration episodes, their overlap with evaluation scenes, or a complete threshold selection procedure. The appendix specifies schemas, voting and fallback, access predicates, parser thresholds and the Table 12 protocol.
content.title: Response to Reviewer Zi51 [1/2]

content.comment:
##  Q1: VLM monitoring versus fixed monitoring
> **Q1:** With the final tool and access stack held fixed, what is the gain from instruction-conditioned monitoring over a fixed or keyword-based monitoring policy? Please clarify how the Table 12 control differs from the final system; a targeted matched comparison would be particularly informative.

The VLM infers whether to record, where the evidence appears, and which entities to monitor. The fixed alternative always records, selects live/video evidence using explicit video/demonstration words, and matches named red/green/blue cubes. Retrieval and repetition specifications remain unchanged. On 200 matched Permanence episodes, fixed monitoring reaches 78.0%, versus 75.5% for VLM monitoring.

The fixed rule is restricted to predefined words and appearance categories, interpreting references outside that vocabulary requires rule extensions. The VLM instead supplies a language-based specification interface.
content.title: Response to Reviewer Zi51 [2/2]

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the motivation for maintaining task-relevant state, the modest inference overhead, and the value of the RecentN baselines and paired comparisons. We address the questions about attribution, reproducibility, and evaluation below. We look forward to discussing the results with the reviewer.

## W1 / W4: Added perception and attribution of task-level gains
> **W1:** The headline comparison is not memory-vs-no-memory within one system. SimpleARM does not merely add a memory layer: it adds an entire frozen perception stack and control interface that the comparison baselines do not possess. 
> **W4:** Table 1's "required state" labels are explicitly not mutually exclusive and are derived from task semantics; several of the largest wins (VideoUnmask 96.0 vs 32.7) have no corresponding ablation, so the biggest contributors to the headline are the least attributed.

The +22.66-point comparison against FrameSamp is a complete-system comparison. To isolate added historical state, we retained the frozen hierarchy, its demonstration inputs and current-view refinement and disabled the additional task-history records/corrections. Success changes from **523/800 (65.38%) to 276/800 (34.50%)**, with 282 full-only and 35 history-disabled-only successes. The within-system difference is **30.88 points**.

This effect is concentrated where maintained history is useful: PatternLock loses 82 points, SwingXtimes 64, ButtonUnmask 56, VideoUnmaskSwap 52, and the reference tasks 36–46. VideoUnmask ablation was also already included in the original demonstration-binding removal (48/50→44/50) in main paper Figure 3.


## W2: Evaluation seeds versus training runs
> **W2:** RecentN+ModuL variants are each trained once and evaluated at three policy seeds, so the three rounds are not independent training runs and cannot estimate training variance.

RoboMME evaluates averages FrameSamp+ModuL variants using the last three checkpoints across three evaluation seeds. The [public FrameSamp release](https://huggingface.co/Yinpei/perceptual-framesamp-modul/tree/main) provides checkpoint **79999**, rather than the full checkpoint set used for that average. Our local re-evaluation of this released FrameSamp+ModuL checkpoint at step 79999 achieves **46.12% (369/800)**, close to the published **44.51%** in RoboMME paper, supporting consistency of the evaluation setup and released checkpoint. Our reported standard deviation measures **evaluation variability, not training variability**. 

## W3: Code, models and prompts
> **W3:** There is no code/model/prompt availability statement anywhere I could find

Model identities are specified in §3.4 and Appendix A.3, including RoboMME’s released GroundSG checkpoint 79999 and Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct adapter checkpoint 1200. Appendix A.1 clarifies that memory planning reuses the same base VLM with its adapter disabled. We have expanded the reproducibility statement and added verbatim prompts, decoding settings. Model weights and simulator assets come from the upstream releases.


## Q1: Multi-seed ablations
> **Q1:** Please re-run no route state and agent-decided access at 2–3 policy seeds, so the central specificity claim does not rest on a single seed. 

Both ablations use frozen weights and **800 matched episode pairs per evaluation seed**. The table reports the change in overall success across all 16 tasks (ablated minus full, in percentage points). The SD measures variability across evaluation seeds for the frozen weights.

| Comparison | Seed 7 | Seed 11 | Seed 23 | Mean ± SD |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| No route state | −7.38 | −11.50 | −8.25 | **−9.04 ± 2.17** |
| Agent-decided access | −10.88 | −11.88 | −9.50 | **−10.75 ± 1.19** |

The appendix gives the task-level effects for both ablations.


## Q2: Colour dependence
> **Q2:** How much of the Permanence gain depends on colour-based identity? A short probe with colour-neutral or colour-relabelled objects would tell the reader whether the maintained "identity" is semantic or chromatic.

Colour is an explicit task reference in RoboMME, e.g., “the container hiding the green cube.” It identifies the cube before occlusion; the subsequent decision requires its remembered relation to a container, whose appearance no longer reveals the hidden colour. With current-view refinement retained, removing added history reduces ButtonUnmask **80% to 24%** and ButtonUnmaskSwap **52% to 16%**, supporting a contribution beyond current-view colour grounding. Our identity initialization nevertheless uses calibrated colour predicates. These results establish memory utility within the benchmark's appearance vocabulary, not robustness to unseen palettes or colour-neutral identity cues, which remain untested.
content.title: Response to Reviewer sSca

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the distinction between maintaining state and using it for control, and for recognizing the value of the episode-matched FrameSamp comparison and the failure analysis. We address the questions about interface dependence, attribution, and transfer below. We look forward to discussing these findings with the reviewer.

## W1 / Q1: Interface dependence and rewording
> **W1:** The dependence on RoboMME's interface still bothers me. Appendix A.1 describes lexical tests on the subgoal text, and A.3 uses calibrated colour predicates and event parsers. In Figure 12, the parser reads pure-red demonstration cues and maps directions through a fixed camera convention. Instruction rewording costs 17.8 points in Table 12. This is a separate configuration, so it needs some caution, but the size of the loss is concerning. The evidence is stronger for this particular RoboMME implementation than for carrying the instruction-conditioned memory layer to a new task family. I would find a small held-out test with unchanged parsers more useful here than simply another large benchmark.
> **Q1:** Can you separate failures in planner output from failures in the structural reader under instruction rewording? I would like to see a matched test with the final configuration fixed.

**Memory-side paraphrase test.** Across 800 matched episodes, success drops from **523/800 (65.38%)** with canonical instructions to **488/800 (61.00%)** with rewording (−4.38 points, 92 canonical-only and 57 rewrite-only successes, exact McNemar $p=0.0052$).

Each of 16 tasks uses two rewrite templates (25 episodes each). We checked the manifest for preserved objects, counts, order and event references. Runtime assertions check canonical environment and composer inputs. Only specification and repetition queries receive the rewrite. Demonstration parsers retain canonical text. The retrieval compiler votes over responses to three line wrappings of one prompt.

**Structural access diagnostic.** We selected ten logged coordinate subgoals spanning seven historical references and three current-view actions. With coordinates and memory held fixed, canonical and syntax-compatible wording match **10/10** intended decisions. Reordered wording misses all seven historical references and correctly skips retrieval in the three current-view cases (**3/10**).

**Relation to Table 12.** The earlier pre-unified system pooled **416 matched pairs** from four handwritten templates per episode on **8 tasks × 13 episodes** at seed 7. Its runtime substitution rebound colours and recognised counts and could fall back to canonical text. The current test passes literal, episode-specific rewrites to the final unified system over all 16 tasks. The two effects (**−17.8** and **−4.38 points**) come from different implementations, rewrites and episode sets.




## W2 / Q2: Same-system history removal and remaining attribution

> **W2:** It is also difficult to assign the full 22.66-point gain to memory, since the system adds perception and subgoal correction. As the authors note, VideoUnmask and BinFill are not very sensitive to the tested removals. Neither the PickHighlight mark reader nor current-view grounding has a separate ablation. The matched removals support several specific mechanisms, but leave part of the system-level gain unexplained. The final component removals use only policy seed 11; the separate identity-tool and no-flow comparisons omit SAM, and the matched FrameSamp runs use different hosts. The paper is careful to document these distinctions. They make me put much more weight on the large effects localized to the relevant tasks than on the small differences.
> **Q2:** How much improvement remains with the same perception and grounding tools but persistent memory disabled? A separate mark-reader removal would also help identify which gains come from history.

Removing SimpleARM's persistent task state and its subgoal corrections reduces success from **523/800 to 276/800 (−30.88 points)**, with 282 full-only and 35 removal-only successes. The frozen composer and VLA, native demonstration and subgoal context, current-view detector refinement and segment coordinate cache remain. Historical identity verification has no stored anchors in this control.




##  Q3: New compositions with unchanged parsers 
> **Q3:** For a held-out task using the same objects in a new combination of historical relations, what would need to change in the schema, event predicates or access rules?

For a new combination of supported relations, the instruction-derived specification would need to select the relevant entities and retrieval operations. A new relation would require a schema field and a predicate for observing it. A new subgoal format would require a compatible access rule.

papers.title: Probing Material Cues in Video Foundation Models
papers.abstract: General-purpose video foundation models (VidFMs) generate realistic videos that capture how surface appearance evolves across viewpoints and illumination conditions, suggesting that their internal representations may encode intrinsic material information even without explicit material supervision. Motivated by this observation, we investigate the material information embedded in pretrained VidFMs through a lightweight probing framework. We keep the foundation models frozen and measure how well material properties can be recovered from their intermediate representations. Through systematic experiments across synthetic and real-world scenes, together with feature-source ablations, we find that VidFM features provide material cues beyond those available from strong image representations. In controlled settings requiring fine-grained material discrimination, video features show a pronounced advantage over DINOv2 features, while the two representations provide complementary information in more complex scenes. Further analyses show that material recoverability benefits from broader viewpoint coverage and is influenced by object-level semantics. Qualitative synthetic-to-real results further suggest that these material cues remain useful beyond the supervised training domain. Together, these findings provide evidence that large-scale video generative models learn reusable representations containing material-relevant information and characterize the conditions under which these representations offer advantages over image features.

content.paper_summary:
The paper proposes to estimate the properties of a digital material model using frozen video models. The idea is to probe the video model intermediate representation to extract the typical channels of a material model, namely albedo, normal, roughness and conductivity. The key message is that large general purpose video models are more efficient than specialized feed forward methods trained from annoted data sets.   
The paper give a comprehensive description of the proposed architecture in its main text, completed well by the apprendices. The validation, although often narrowed to "DINO vs video features" is quite complete. 
I think the main contribution is in the use of frozen video features, optionally fused with DINO feature, to estimate material properties. I think this is an interesting research direction. But I lack elements to really assess how the proposed approach compare to direct specialized methods, both in speed/resolution and quality.
content.critical_strengths:
1/ The paper makes an interesting point in that video features can be very informative for material recognition and estimation. 
2/ The fusion of Dino features with the video ones is quite interesting and could certainly be pushed further in the future, although not so critical in the experiment numbers for now.
content.critical_weaknesses:
1/ I think the specialized e.g., feed forward material estimation methods are too quickly discarded. First, this a vast body of work that would deserve a bit more of discussion. Second, although there is certainly interest in knowing how far video models features can go to solve the task, it would still be very informative so see a more comprehensive comparison to specialized models.

2/ While I like the idea of fusing video features, I wonder whether exploiting the training data to adapt Dino feature (fine tuning, LoRA, etc) would help making the them more useful in the fused case. 

I believe there are some citation issues (Zeng/Zheng?)
content.questions_for_authors:
1/ Would DINOv3 provide any improvement?
2/ Instead of keeping DINO frozen, would an adaptation performed using the same data used to train heads, help improving the DINO side of the feature extraction?
3/ There are other ways to use video models for the task, e.g. VideoNeuMat; how do they compare (at least at a high level) to the proposed method in term of final material appearance (beyond the actual PBR vs neural format)?

content.paper_summary:
- This paper investigates whether the frozen internal representations of a pretrained general-purpose video foundation model (VidFM) can be reconstructed to capture PBR material properties (albedo, roughness, metallicity, and normal). The authors extract features from CogVideoX, OpenSora, and WAN, and predict material maps using trainable projectors and probes. Compare with the DINOv2 and material-estimation baselines on the Ball, RoomTour, and DL3DV datasets.
- The key finding is that WAN-only features recover roughness and metallicity much better than DINOv2-only features in the Ball dataset. In RoomTour, WAN-only is not superior to DINOv2-only across all properties, but combining WAN and DINOv2 yields the best results. The authors argue that this means VidFM representations include material-related cues and can be complementary to image features in complex scenes.
content.critical_strengths:
- The research question is clear: to directly measure to what extent material-related information is present in pretrained video representations.
- We distinguish between the results of material estimation and representation analysis, comparing feature sources over a frozen backbone.
- Distinguishes synthetic ground-truth data from pseudo-label-based real-world data and identifies the numerical limitations of DL3DV.
- By presenting results for WAN-only, DINOv2-only, and fused features together, we aim to partially distinguish the effects of feature fusion from those of the WAN feature itself.
content.critical_weaknesses:
- **There is no basis for VidFM's standalone feature aside from WAN.** The video-only feature-source comparison in Table 1 includes WAN only. Since the main-table results from CogVideoX and OpenSora are feature results fused with DINOv2, it is not possible to conclude that the individual features of each model contain material-relevant information based solely on these results.
- **The effects of temporal pretraining are not dissociated.** The backbones compared in the paper differ in architecture, pretraining data, model scale, and learning objective. Therefore, the current experiment only shows differences in performance between pretrained representations; there is no evidence that temporal modeling or video pretraining created those differences.
- **The basis for real-world material accuracy is limited.** The figure for DL3DV is the agreement with pseudo-labels, and the authors also state that it is not definitive physical ground truth. The synthetic-to-real evaluation is a qualitative comparison of 10 YouTube videos, and a ground-truth material map is not provided. Therefore, no strong conclusions regarding the accuracy of the actual material or generalization are supported by the current evidence.
content.questions_for_authors:
- **Practical significance of the analysis.** This paper presents the analytical observation that material information can be recovered from the frozen VidFM feature. However, based on the current results alone, it is unclear what specific benefits this observation would lead to in the design or practical use of the material estimation model. The authors should either clearly demonstrate that this material recoverability analysis provides practical knowledge or design principles beyond simple probing results, or limit the paper's contribution and claims to the scope of analytical observations. **This is an important factor in assessing the core contribution and impact of this paper.**
- Can CogVideoX and OpenSora also produce video-only feature results without DINOv2 fusion? If not, are you willing to limit the statement that all VidFMs provide material-relevant features on their own?

content.paper_summary: The paper investigates recoverability of material properties from frozen video foundation model features. Intermediate diffusion activations are optionally fused with DINOv2 features and decoded by a supervised multiframe probe. Evaluation uses synthetic Ball and RoomTour data with PBR ground truth and DL3DV with pseudo annotations. WAN-only features substantially outperform DINOv2 on Ball roughness and metallicity, while their fusion improves all three material properties on RoomTour; other video backbones are evaluated in the fused setting. Relighting and qualitative synthetic-to-real tests provide downstream checks.
content.critical_strengths:
**Broad experimental coverage and complementary validation.**
The evaluation covers three general-purpose video backbones across Ball, RoomTour, and DL3DV, alongside image-based and material-adapted baselines. This breadth helps characterize how material recoverability varies across backbones and scene settings. Feature-source ablations examine the contribution and complementarity of video and image representations. The downstream evaluation also compares VidFM-MatHead with MVInverse and DiffusionRenderer fine-tuned on the authors’ datasets, providing additional evidence of the full system’s utility for material reconstruction.
content.critical_weaknesses:
**Limited novelty beyond an empirical task extension.**
The core probe closely resembles Huang et al. (2025). The shift from geometric outputs to material maps, together with DINOv2 fusion, appears primarily to adapt this established framework to a new task. The Method section should explicitly distinguish shared design choices from material-specific modifications.
The broad comparisons establish useful material-specific empirical findings, particularly recoverability and image–video complementarity. However, the additional analyses offer limited explanation of why the video features help. These findings leave the contribution predominantly empirical, with limited additional methodological or explanatory novelty.
content.questions_for_authors:
- Figure 14 and Table 2 show substantial backbone-dependent differences on RoomTour. What explains why WAN features improve roughness and metallicity estimation over DINOv2, whereas OpenSora and CogVideoX features do not, despite using the same probing architecture and DINOv2 fusion? What material-specific insight can be drawn from these contrasting results?
- VidFM-MatHead’s predicted material maps appear to exhibit mild temporal flickering in the supplementary video. Have similar fluctuations been observed in the WAN-only probe?

papers.title: BrainSaber: Reconstruction-Based Information Decomposition for Functional Brain Atlas Construction
papers.abstract: Brain atlases define the regional units through which we study brain function. Yet parcellation based on signal or representational similarity does not explicitly distinguish how locations share information or jointly predict activity elsewhere. We introduce BrainSaber, a whole-brain atlas framework built on our proposed reconstruction-based information decomposition RID. RID uses controlled masking of a frozen, pretrained fMRI autoencoder to compare reconstructions of common targets from individual and paired sources. It distinguishes redundant, unique, and synergistic predictive contributions through shared, source-specific, and joint-only reconstruction successes. BrainSaber combines these components with brain-wide predictive flow and spatial constraints to construct contiguous parcels across cortical and non-cortical structures. Regional analyses reveal contrasting associations of redundancy and synergy with conventional functional connectivity. Exploratory cortical and whole-brain evaluations show favorable parcel homogeneity and separability, while prediction across five datasets and cross-window and cross-session analyses support downstream utility and group-atlas repeatability. These findings motivate information composition as a complementary basis for functional parcellation, extending similarity-based grouping to account for individual and joint predictive contributions.

papers.title: GroundedVCoT: Grounding Interleaved Text-Image Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Visual intelligence requires reasoning about how a scene changes and using the resulting state to guide later decisions. Unified multimodal models can make this  explicit by interleaving textual reasoning with generated images. Yet generated images also enter the context for later steps. If any generated image misrepresents an action or contradicts the text, the error can compound across the trajectory. We introduce GroundedVCoT, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework for grounding interleaved text--image chain-of-thought. At each step, task-specific verifiers assess textual claims and generated visual states against the state implied by the model's own decisions. Step-wise grounding rewards and task success yield a shared advantage that updates both text and image policies. Verification follows the model's trajectory, allowing alternative valid solutions while preserving its self-generated visual history. We evaluate three distinct demands on visual reasoning: planning moves in Rush Hour, constructing a semantic figure in Tangram, and tracking rotations in Rolling Dice. Relative to supervised fine-tuning, GroundedVCoT raises Rush Hour solve rate from 48.0\% to 71.3\% (+23.3\%), Tangram accuracy from 25.6\% to 50.5\% (+24.9\%), and Rolling Dice accuracy from 25.6\% to 60.0\% (+34.4\%), also consistently exceeding terminal reward RL, supporting the value of grounding intermediate steps rather than rewarding task completion alone.

papers.title: ICE: Task-Aligned Clifford Latent Fields for Multimodal Graph Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs connect entities, visual content, language, and observed relations. Learning one foundation across such graphs requires more than compressing each node into a fused Euclidean vector. The representation must preserve entity semantics, construct interaction state from graph neighborhoods, and expose that state to prediction units with different geometry. Our empirical study shows why these requirements are inseparable. Higher-grade channels recover pair relations across the foundation graphs, specialized queries reveal information hidden by a generic readout, and rigid blade isolation removes cross-grade capacity. We therefore introduce ICE (Interaction-aware Clifford Encoder), a multimodal graph foundation model built on a node-indexed Clifford latent field. Topology, text, and images enter explicit Cl(3) addresses. Edge-aware geometric products transform these directions into scalar, bivector, and trivector relations over observed neighborhoods. A protected Grade-1 route preserves entity semantics, while the full grade and depth bank remains available to fresh node and link heads. We establish exact cross-grade reachability, node-permutation equivariance, and a bound on the task residual around the semantic score. Experiments span one shared foundation over eleven graphs, six node-classification datasets, three link-prediction datasets, and matched few-shot tasks. ICE ranks first in all 30 reported supervised and few-shot comparisons. Core removals reduce every task summary, and mechanism controls connect the gains to higher-order transport, retained multidepth structure, semantic protection, and direct field access.

papers.title: PrismQ: Noise-Aware Resource Allocation for Elastic Post-Training Quantization
papers.abstract: Elastic post-training quantization (PTQ) jointly calibrates multiple precisions within a single model, enabling flexible precision adaptation under different deployment budgets. However, extending reconstruction from a single precision to multiple precisions introduces two key challenges. First, quantization errors vary across linear layers and precisions, creating a trade-off between cross-precision parameter sharing and precision-specific reconstruction capacity within the reconstruction space. Second, calibration states should reflect precision-dependent error propagation, while preserving complete quantized states for every precision incurs substantial calibration memory overhead. To address these challenges, we propose PrismQ, a noise-aware elastic PTQ framework that adapts both reconstruction space and calibration states according to precision-dependent quantization errors. Specifically, PrismRank estimates the demand for reconstruction capacity at each linear layer and precision from the singular-value characteristics of clipping-induced errors, and PrismLoRA realizes the resulting capacity allocation through shared and precision-specific low-rank components. Moreover, Calibration-only Sparse Token selects quantized token states according to token-wise quantization error under a fixed cache budget and uses them to construct calibration inputs for the next block, allowing these inputs to reflect precision-dependent error propagation. Extensive experiments on language models, vision transformers, and vision-language models show that PrismQ improves quantization performance across multiple precisions, with particularly clear gains at low bit widths.

papers.title: CoDev-Bench: Can Coding Agents Handle Naturally Concurrent Development?
papers.abstract: Current coding benchmarks usually assume a single developer working on a standalone issue. However, real-world software development is inherently concurrent and collaborative, with multiple developers authoring pull requests (PRs) within the same codebase. To bridge this gap, we introduce CoDev-Bench, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate coding agents on concurrent multi-task resolution. CoDev-Bench involves 206 concurrent PR-pair tasks drawn from 137 production-scale open-source repositories across six languages. Each task consists of two independently authored PRs that branch from a shared base commit and are subsequently integrated into the main branch. The benchmark reflects the complexity of real concurrent development, with an average of 17.1 non-test files and 507 lines of code modified per pair, and 45.1\% of pairs exhibiting file-level overlap.  As reference baselines, we evaluate a single agent that handles both PRs, as well as two multi-agent designs: assigning each PR to a separate agent and merging their patches afterwards, and letting a main agent delegate sub-tasks to sub-agents while it works. Even the best-performing configuration resolves only about one-fifth of tasks on average over three trials, compared with over 80\% for state-of-the-art systems on SWE-Bench Verified, showing that naturally concurrent PR-composition tasks remain a largely unsaturated challenge for current coding agents.

papers.title: Distribution-Guided Classifier-Free Guidance
papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is central to conditional generation with diffusion models, but using a constant guidance strength overlooks how the diffusion rate, signal content, and score reliability vary throughout denoising. We introduce Distribution-Guided CFG (DG-CFG), a training-free schedule that reallocates a fixed guidance budget across timesteps to improve the balance among generation quality, diversity, and stability. A path-integral analysis of deterministic CFG identifies the temporal weight that governs how guidance accumulates along sampling trajectories. Combining this principle with signal-content weighting and error-motivated low-noise attenuation yields a middle-focused schedule that emphasizes informative and reliable stages of denoising. Controlled experiments with analytic scores support the path-integral predictions and illustrate the effect of temporal reweighting. Across different backbones and sampling methods, DG-CFG provides a favorable diversity--fidelity trade-off and improves generation quality under strong guidance while controlling saturation. Component ablations and sampling-budget evaluations further support the schedule design and robustness.
keywords: Classifier-Free Guidance; Diffusion Models; Probability Flow ODE;

papers.title: AURORA-LM: Autoencoding Unified Representation for Continuous-Latent Diffusion Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Continuous latent-space modeling has proved effective for image, video, and audio generation, while text generation is still dominated by models that directly predict discrete tokens. Existing continuous language models often inherit embedding spaces not designed for both generation and decoding, or compress autoencoded latents to ease diffusion, potentially sacrificing token-level fidelity. Instead of simplifying the representation to accommodate the generative model, we introduce AURORA-LM, a continuous-latent diffusion language model that preserves a high-capacity, decodable text latent and learns its distribution separately. A Query-based Encoder-Decoder organizes text into a prefix-aligned latent sequence. We then freeze the autoencoder and train a Block-causal Diffusion Transformer to model these full-width latents through blockwise flow matching. However, retaining these high-dimensional latents makes diffusion modeling more challenging. We address this difficulty by restricting only the noisy-input pathway through a low-rank bottleneck while retaining the full clean-latent prediction target, and calibrating the noise-level distribution to the latent width. Finally, we introduce self-trajectory consistency to bridge the gap between training on independently sampled noisy states and inference through iterative denoising. AURORA-LM achieves the best Gen-PPL and MAUVE on OpenWebText free generation and the best ROUGE scores on XSum conditional summarization among the evaluated continuous and diffusion-based language models. Scaling its denoiser to 1B parameters, it also outperforms a larger publicly released latent-diffusion language model under matched prompting and scoring.

papers.title: State-Conditioned Invertible Channel Dependencies for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Multivariate time series (MTS) forecasting requires jointly capturing inter-series dependencies and intra-series temporal evolutions. Although inverted Transformers (e.g., iTransformer) and Graph Neural Networks can capture arbitrary pairwise inter-channel dependencies, they typically suffer from unconstrained $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ pairwise attention maps that are prone to overfitting spurious cross-channel correlations. Furthermore, aggregating multiple channels into a weighted sum risks destructive signal cancellation and over-smoothing across distinct channels. To address these limitations, we propose a State-conditioned Invertible Channel Dependencies Network (SICDNet) that comprises two dedicated components: Structured Invertible Channel Mixer (SICM) for inter-series correlation modeling and the Spectral-Gated Modulator (SGM) for intra-series feature extraction. SICM establishes pairwise channel interactions on latent features using a dyadic pairing schedule, which adopts a multi-stage, multi-round cascade with cyclic node-index shifts to cover more cross-channel pairs. Specifically, SICM groups the latent representations and executes Givens rotations within each paired channels of each group, and the rotation angles are conditioned dynamically based on pairwise energy. SICM is energy-preserving and mathematically invertible, enabling the extraction of robust inter-channel correlations. Complementarily, SGM combines static harmonic priors with data-dependent dynamic spectral gating and dual-domain gated fusion, adaptively capturing global periodic patterns. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that SICDNet reduces the inter-series mixing complexity from $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ while maintaining channel-independent linear scaling in intra-series spectral processing, outperforming dense attention and graph estimation architectures.

papers.title: CFPP: Conflict-Free Preservation Projection for Locate-then-Edit Model Editing
papers.abstract: Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in large language models (LLMs) after deployment, without retraining the full model. A widely used locate-then-edit paradigm localizes critical MLP representations and computes a targeted parameter update. However, its preservation term can penalize edit-relevant directions when the dominant subspace of its covariance overlaps with the active edit subspace. This preservation–edit conflict becomes more severe as the number of edits grows, leading to under-editing and degraded generalization. We propose CFPP (Conflict-Free Preservation Projection), a lightweight framework that modifies the preservation covariance before computing the local closed-form update. CFPP stabilizes the edit geometry through spectral whitening and applies residual-aware soft projection with trace calibration to attenuate edit-aligned components while maintaining the overall preservation budget. CFPP is designed for locate-then-edit methods such as MEMIT, PMET, and EAMET. Experiments on GPT2-XL, Mistral-7B, and LLaMA3-8B show that CFPP yields an average relative gain of 8.2\% in the reported Avg. score, with improvements reaching 31.5\% in individual settings. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CFPP-B4H7.

papers.title: Fix What's Wrong, Keep What's Right: Hallucination Repair for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored to automate operations research modeling, reduce modeling time and lower the expertise barrier to optimization based decision support. However, this process often introduces inconsistencies between generated artifacts and the original problem, which we refer to as optimization modeling hallucinations. Despite progress in general-purpose hallucination mitigation, optimization modeling poses a distinct repair challenge: restoring fidelity to the original problem through coordinated model–code updates. We introduce OPT-Kraken, a training-free hallucination repair framework. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first post-hoc framework for repairing hallucinations in LLM-based optimization modeling artifacts. It extracts problem requirements and instance data, localizes errors by checking problem–model fidelity, model–code consistency, and data grounding, and selects repair granularity by the affected scope. For local repair, category rules and instance evidence are compiled into contracts specifying permitted edits, expected effects, and protected content. Experiments on established optimization modeling benchmarks show positive gains across automatic modeling frameworks and fine-tuned models. On zero-shot artifacts from multiple base models, OPT-Kraken effectively repairs optimization modeling hallucinations while preserving initially correct artifacts. These results demonstrate effective and controlled repair for LLM-based optimization modeling artifacts.
keywords: Large Language Models; Optimization Modeling; Operations Research; Hallucination Repair; Evidence-Constrained Repair

papers.title: AlphaRouter: An Expert Routing Approach for Adaptive Portfolio Selection
papers.abstract: Portfolio selection requires adapting asset allocations to changing market conditions while controlling risk and satisfying investment constraints. Existing learning-based methods often predict asset weights directly from market data, making portfolio decisions sensitive to noisy and nonstationary observations. We propose \textbf{AlphaRouter}, an adaptive portfolio selection framework that separates portfolio construction from market-dependent selection. AlphaRouter maintains a set of complementary experts, each capturing distinct historical market patterns to produce a complete portfolio under shared investment constraints.
